title: Adrenal Glands Anatomy
descriptor: Position, Cortex & Medulla, Blood Supply, Stress Hormones, Adrenal Disorders
intro: The adrenal glands are a pair of small, triangular endocrine glands, one lying on the upper surface of each kidney. Each has an outer cortex that makes steroid hormones such as cortisol and aldosterone, and an inner medulla that makes adrenaline and noradrenaline for the fight-or-flight response. Together they help the body respond to stress and regulate salt and water balance.

keyFacts.label: Location
keyFacts.value: On the upper surface of each kidney, within the renal (Gerota's) fascia

keyFacts.label: Shape
keyFacts.value: Triangular overall; the right gland is pyramid-like and the left more crescent-shaped

keyFacts.label: Layers
keyFacts.value: Outer cortex in three zones and inner medulla, within a connective tissue capsule

keyFacts.label: Cortex hormones
keyFacts.value: Aldosterone (outer zone), cortisol (middle zone) and androgens (inner zone)

keyFacts.label: Arterial supply
keyFacts.value: Superior suprarenal (from the inferior phrenic), middle suprarenal and renal artery branches

keyFacts.label: Venous drainage
keyFacts.value: One vein per gland; the left drains into the left renal vein

sections.heading: Location and relations
sections.body:
Each adrenal gland is a small, triangular organ that sits on the upper surface of a kidney, within the renal (Gerota's) fascia. The glands are also known as the suprarenal glands. The two glands differ in shape: the right gland is pyramid-like, whereas the left has a more crescent-like form. The right gland lies close to the liver, behind the inferior vena cava and in front of the diaphragm.

The two layers of each gland have different embryonic origins: the cortex is derived from mesoderm, whereas the medulla is derived from neural crest cells.

sections.heading: Cortex and medulla
sections.body: Each gland has an outer cortex of glandular tissue and an inner medulla of nervous tissue, all surrounded by a connective tissue capsule. The cortex is organised into three zones, and each zone makes a different class of steroid hormone from cholesterol. The outermost zona glomerulosa makes mineralocorticoids, mainly aldosterone, which affect fluid and electrolyte balance. The middle zona fasciculata makes glucocorticoids, chiefly cortisol, which affect glucose metabolism. The innermost zona reticularis releases only small amounts of androgens, which may supplement the sex hormones released from the gonads. The medulla at the core of the gland makes the amine hormones adrenaline (epinephrine) and noradrenaline (norepinephrine), and adrenaline is the main one.

sections.heading: Blood supply and nerves
sections.body: The adrenal glands are highly vascular. Arterial blood reaches each gland from several sources: the superior suprarenal arteries (branches of the inferior phrenic arteries), the middle suprarenal arteries, and a contribution from the renal artery on the same side. Each gland is drained by a single adrenal vein that emerges at its hilum. On the left, the adrenal vein drains into the left renal vein, because the left gland lies farther from the inferior vena cava. The medulla receives preganglionic sympathetic nerve fibres, which release acetylcholine to stimulate the release of adrenaline and noradrenaline.

sections.heading: Hormones and their control
sections.body:
The medulla drives the short-term fight-or-flight response: adrenaline, together with noradrenaline, prepares the body for action and is released in response to sympathetic nervous system signals. The cortex drives the long-term response, through a pathway that runs from the hypothalamus, through ACTH released from the anterior pituitary, to the release of cortisol from the cortex.

Cortisol regulates a wide range of processes, including metabolism and the immune response, and has an important role in helping the body respond to stress. As cortisol levels rise, they slow the release of corticotrophin-releasing hormone from the hypothalamus and of ACTH from the pituitary, which forms a feedback loop. Aldosterone's main role is to regulate salt and water in the body, which affects blood pressure. The renin-angiotensin system also drives aldosterone release, because angiotensin II stimulates the zona glomerulosa to make aldosterone.

sections.heading: Clinical relevance: underactive adrenal glands
sections.body: Adrenal problems can arise when the glands are overactive or underactive. In Addison's disease, also called primary adrenal insufficiency, the glands are underactive and lack the hormones usually made by the cortex: cortisol, aldosterone and androgens. Damage to the cortex lowers hormone output, and in developed countries autoimmune disease is the usual cause. Early symptoms can resemble depression or flu and include fatigue, muscle weakness, loss of appetite and weight loss, and darkening of the skin is a distinguishing feature. An adrenal crisis, in which symptoms get worse very quickly, can be triggered by an infection, an injury or surgery and needs emergency care.

sections.heading: Clinical relevance: excess hormones and tumours
sections.body:
Cushing's syndrome is caused by too much cortisol in the body. Long-term high-dose steroid medicine is the most common trigger, and a non-cancerous growth on the pituitary or adrenal gland can also cause it; when the pituitary is responsible it is called Cushing's disease. Features include weight gain, a rounded red face, easy bruising, stretch marks and muscle weakness.

In primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome), an adrenal gland releases too much aldosterone, most often because of a non-cancerous adrenal tumour, and blood pressure can become very high. Cancer can also arise in the gland: for adrenocortical carcinoma, surgery to remove the adrenal gland (adrenalectomy) is often used. Phaeochromocytoma is a tumour of the adrenal gland that releases excess adrenaline and noradrenaline and can cause intense episodes lasting a short time, known as paroxysmal attacks.

sections.heading: How the adrenal glands are investigated
sections.body: Because symptoms such as fatigue and weakness are non-specific, they need assessment by a clinician. In suspected Addison's disease, blood tests measure sodium, potassium and cortisol. The ACTH stimulation test is the test used most often to diagnose adrenal insufficiency, and blood tests can also detect antibodies in autoimmune Addison's disease. For suspected Cushing's syndrome, cortisol can be checked in blood, urine or saliva, and a high result leads to referral to an endocrinologist, who may arrange further blood tests and scans. Diagnosis is based on the medical history, a physical examination and laboratory tests.
